passage: The review meeting at the ward office ended, and Hemant sat back down with the composting report open. 'Total flop,' he muttered. Omkar, from the accounts desk, pulled up a chair. 'Flop out of ten, or flop out of what?' Hemant almost laughed. On the whiteboard he drew a line from 0 to 10. Collection from the two big colonies: steady every week, so maybe a 7. Bins in the market lane: broken twice, smelly, a 3. Volunteer turnout: strong for a month, then gone, a 4. He wrote two columns, Kept Going and Fell Apart, and the second was shorter than he expected. 'So it's a five, not a zero,' Omkar said. Hemant circled the market lane. 'And this is what the next round fixes first.'

qa.a: The bins in the market lane, which broke twice and were smelly, got a 3.

qa.q: Why did 'total flop' feel true to Hemant right after the review meeting?
qa.a: Hemant was frustrated and discouraged after the meeting, so the problems filled his mind and one bad part seemed to stand for the whole drive.

qa.q: What choice turned Hemant's review from a verdict into a plan?
qa.a: Drawing a 0-to-10 line and making two columns let him score each part on its own, so he could see the colonies were working and pick the market lane as the first fix.

qa.q: How might Omkar see Hemant's shift from 'flop' to 'five'?
qa.a: Omkar likely finds this far more useful: a flat 'flop' gave the team nothing to act on, while a five with one clear first fix gives everyone a next step.

grounding: Shows an adult who dismissed a whole project as a flop rescoring each part on a 0-to-10 line and finding a middle rating with a clear next step.

Dear Shalini,
On Sunday night I typed 'the book fair was a disaster' to you and then deleted it. I'm glad I did. This morning I tried your trick and gave it a mark out of ten instead.
Footfall: 6. We hoped for four hundred people and about two hundred and fifty came.

Love,
Lalremsiami

passage: People kept asking me, 'Bhupen, how did the screening go?' And I kept saying, 'Total waste of a year.' Alka, I said it at the bus stop, I said it to Ma, I said it to the mirror. passage:
My roommate Nilesh spent two months planning his first home-bakery stall at the Sunday flea market in Pune. On the day, it drizzled, half the crowd never came, and he carried three boxes of unsold brownies back up our stairs.

"Total disaster," he said, dropping onto the sofa. "I'm not a baker. I'm a guy who wasted two months."

Then he went quiet and frowned at the ceiling. "No. Disaster is too big a word." He took a flattened pizza box and drew a line from one to ten. Sales: four. The lemon cake sold out in an hour, so that was a nine. Stall set-up: two, because the banner kept blowing into people's faces. Price cards: seven.

I didn't say much. I just watched him make two lists, "Keep" and "Change", in black marker. The "Keep" list was longer.

"So maybe a five," he said. "And next time, a heavier banner and more lemon cake."

— Tarun

qa.q: What sold out in an hour at Nilesh's stall?
qa.a: The lemon cake sold out in an hour.

qa.q: Why did "total disaster" feel accurate to Nilesh as he dropped onto the sofa?
qa.a: He was tired, wet and carrying three boxes of unsold brownies, so the losses were all he could see. After two months of planning, anything less than success felt like wasted time.

qa.q: What was the turning point, and why did the scale help?
qa.a: The turning point was when Nilesh caught himself and said disaster was too big a word. Rating each part from one to ten showed what worked, like the lemon cake, and gave clear fixes for next time.

qa.q: How might Tarun have felt watching Nilesh go from "disaster" to "maybe a five"?
qa.a: Tarun was probably relieved to see a friend stop beating himself up without needing to be argued out of it. Staying quiet and just watching let Nilesh do the rethinking himself.

grounding: A roommate watches a young man catch himself calling his market stall a disaster, then rate each part on a scale and list what worked and what to change.

passage: Sit, Ishita, the chai can wait. You're calling this launch a disaster, and it reminds me of the library project I ran at twenty-five, the first one with my name on top. We set up reading corners in six municipal schools. By the end of the term only two were still being used, and I walked into my manager's cabin ready to say the whole thing had failed. Before I could, I caught the word in my own mouth. Failed? Everything? So I took a sheet and wrote one to ten for each part. Book selection, eight; the children loved the comics. Teacher training, three; we did one session and left. Storage, two; the monsoon soaked the shelves. Mr Dsouza looked at the sheet and said, 'Pema, this is a report, not a funeral.' That sheet became the plan for the next year, and the two corners that worked taught us why the other four didn't. So give me your numbers, part by part.

I'm Abhinav, and last summer my friend Mohit and I ran a weekend dosa stall at the Koramangala flea market. After the last Sunday, sitting in an auto with a crate of unused batter, I said, "That was a complete disaster. We should never have tried."

Mohit said, "Rate it. One to ten."

I wanted to say one. But then I actually thought. We sold out on two Saturdays. People came back for the podi dosa. Our tawa was too small, we never worked out the queue, and the rain on the last weekend killed us.

I said, "Maybe five?"

He said, "Then write the five good things and the five bad ones." We did it on the back of the menu card. On paper, it wasn't a disaster. It was a first try. This year we're back, with two tawas.

qa.q: Where did Abhinav and Mohit run the dosa stall?
qa.a: They ran it at the Koramangala flea market.

qa.q: What was Abhinav feeling in the auto with the unused batter?
qa.a: Abhinav felt disappointed and deflated, and in that mood the whole stall seemed a complete disaster.

qa.q: Why did rating and listing help Abhinav?
qa.a: It revealed the grey: good things like repeat customers and sold-out Saturdays beside fixable problems like the small tawa, which made room to try again.

qa.q: How might Mohit have felt hearing "We should never have tried"?
qa.a: Mohit may have felt a little stung, since it was their shared project, but chose to help Abhinav see it more fairly.

Supervisor's note, water project, Latur, 4 November.

After Friday's review, Jagdish told me the rainwater tank pilot was "a total failure" and asked to be taken off it. He was pale and had clearly not slept.

I asked him to rate the pilot from one to ten instead of pass or fail. He said two. Then I asked him to list, in two columns, what worked and what didn't. Worked: eleven of fifteen tanks built on time; the village committee now meets weekly; the women's group keeps the logbook. Didn't: four tanks leak at the joints, and the pipe order came late.

By the end he said, "Maybe six." We agreed he stays on the project, with one job this month: find out why the joints leak.

I'll check in with him on Wednesday.

Nirmala

qa.q: How many tanks were built on time?
qa.a: Eleven of fifteen tanks were built on time.

qa.q: Why did Jagdish ask to be taken off the project?
qa.a: Jagdish felt ashamed and discouraged after the review, and saw the whole pilot as a total failure.

qa.q: What did Nirmala's two columns make possible?
qa.a: They showed real successes beside fixable problems, moving the rating from two to six and giving Jagdish one clear job: find out why the joints leak.

qa.q: How might the village committee see the pilot?
qa.a: The committee likely sees real progress, since they now meet weekly and have working tanks, even with four leaking.

grounding: A supervisor's note shows a young engineer who calls a pilot a total failure and is helped to rate it and list what worked.

Sunday night
The community book fair is over and my first thought on the walk home was: total failure. Forty people came instead of the two hundred we hoped for. The children's corner ran out of chairs. It rained at four.
Then I caught myself. "Total" is a big word. Alka always asks me to score things out of ten, so I sat down with tea and did it.
Honest score: five out of ten.
What worked: the storytelling hour was full. We sold ninety books. Three new volunteers signed up. The old librarian cried when a girl asked for poetry.
What didn't: posters went up too late. No shelter plan for rain. Too few chairs.
Next time: posters two weeks earlier, a tarpaulin, borrow chairs from the temple hall.
Five out of ten doesn't feel like failure. It feels like a first try.
Francis

qa.a: Forty people came instead of the two hundred they hoped for.

qa.q: How did Francis feel on the walk home, and what changed that feeling?
qa.a: Francis felt deflated and sure it was a total failure, then calmer after scoring it out of ten and listing what worked.

qa.q: Which of Francis's next-time ideas is the most practical first step?
qa.a: Putting posters up two weeks earlier, since late posters probably explain much of the low turnout.

qa.a: Alka would likely feel pleased that the scoring habit helped, and could add ideas to the list for the next fair.

The garden-plot booking site Emil's team had built for the Copenhagen library went live on Monday. By Wednesday only forty people had signed up, and Emil told Abebe over coffee, "It's a total failure. Six months, wasted."
